query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The stability of equimolar HEA nanoparticles during high‐temperature catalytic/thermoelectric operation is governed by a balance between high configurational entropy and lattice distortion–induced kinetic stabilization. Under inert or reducing atmospheres, the severe lattice distortions (arising from atomic size mismatches within 15%) elevate an 'effective temperature' that kinetically hinders phase separation and surface segregation, thus maintaining the initial solid solution structure. In contrast, under oxidizing atmospheres, enhanced surface chemical driving forces can partially overcome this kinetic barrier, leading to limited surface segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.intervention: Heating the nanoparticles in situ (using TEM or high‐temperature XRD) under controlled atmospheres (inert, reducing, and oxidizing) across the 473–1923 K operating range.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted over 473–1923 K with controlled atmospheres; the hypothesis holds when the constituent elements have atomic size differences within ~15% and when the processing times are sufficient to capture kinetic effects without allowing complete equilibrium segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortions due to atomic size mismatches and the associated high-density overlapping energy barriers, which raise the effective kinetic barrier for phase separation.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes the random solid solution while lattice distortions reduce atomic diffusivity, thus providing a kinetic barrier against phase separation and chemical ordering. Under oxidizing conditions, surface chemical potential gradients may locally drive limited segregation despite the kinetic stabilization.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under inert and reducing atmospheres, in situ measurements will show the retention of a largely homogeneous solid solution (minimal phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity) relative to the initial state. Under oxidizing conditions, minor surface segregation or rearrangement may be detected, but the core remains thermodynamically stabilized by the kinetic barrier provided by lattice distortion.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized, homogeneous solid solution state at room temperature before exposure to high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold for HEA nanoparticles where the atomic size differences are within an approximate 15% range and under atmospheres that do not impose extreme oxidation potentials. Deviations might occur if the alloy components exhibit greater size mismatch or in environments with very strong oxidizing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative contributions of lattice distortion versus chemical driving forces under varying atmospheres remain uncertain and may vary with specific elemental combinations; further measurements are needed to establish precise thresholds for stability breakdown.

falsification_experiment.design: Using in situ TEM or high-temperature XRD, heat the HEA nanoparticles from room temperature to 1923 K under three atmospheres (inert, reducing, and oxidizing). Monitor the crystal structure, lattice parameters, and compositional homogeneity with time-resolved imaging and spectroscopy techniques.
measurements: Local compositional mapping via EDS or EELS
Quantification of lattice distortions and strain mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant phase separation, chemical ordering, or extensive surface segregation is observed under inert or reducing atmospheres (where kinetic stabilization via lattice distortion should dominate), or if the extent of lattice distortion does not correlate with the observed stability across the temperature range, then the proposed hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have exhibited unusual materials properties. The stability of equimolar single-phase solid solution of five or more elements is supposedly rare and identifying the existence of such alloys has been challenging because of the vast chemical space of possible combinations. Herein, based on high-throughput density-functional theory calculations, we construct a chemical map of single-phase equimolar high-entropy alloys by investigating over 658,000 equimolar quinary alloys through a binary regular solid-solution model. We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures. We unveil the chemistries that are likely to form high-entropy alloys, and identify the complex interplay among mixing enthalpy, intermetallics formation, and melting point that drives the formation of these solid solutions. We demonstrate the power of our method by predicting the existence of two new high-entropy alloys, i.e. the body-centered cubic AlCoMnNiV and the face-centered cubic CoFeMnNiZn, which are successfully synthesized.Subject terms: Materials science, Structure of solids and liquids, Theo

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. In this study, we present in situ atomic-scale evidence that a random solid solution (RSS) structure enables AuCu NWs to exhibit superplasticity with ~260% uniform elongation and ultrahigh strength of ~6 GPa. We discovered that the excellent properties originate from the chemical inhomogeneity (similar to that of high-entropy alloys), which leads to widely distributed and overlapping energy barriers for multiple plasticity mechanisms and enables the AuCu alloy NWs to exhibit several unconventional plastic deformation modes, such as an ultrahigh density of deformation-induced HCP lamellae (including 2H and 4H phases), zigzag-like nanotwins, and reversible FCC–HCP phase transition. These deformation modes hinder the dislocation motion, which ultimately leads to superplasticity and ultrahigh strength in the AuCu NWs.

The escalating issues of the energy crisis and environmental pollution underscore the urgency of the transition to a sustainable global economy. A pivotal aspect of this shift is the advancement of renewable energy technologies, especially those facilitating the conversion of chemical energy to electrical energy in fuel cells. At the heart of these energy conversion devices is the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), whose efficiency is considerably hindered by the dearth of effective electrocatalysts., Platinum (Pt) stands as the most effective pure metal catalyst for the ORR, yet its widespread application is constrained by its high cost and scarcity. Efforts to reduce the loading of precious metals while enhancing site-specific activity have concentrated on the modification of Pt sites with strategies such as defect engineering, core–shell nanostructuring, and near-surface alloying. A major limitation of these Pt-based site ensembles is long-term durability, severely compromised by interfacial processes such as leaching, dealloying, and degradation dynamically occurring under operating conditions.
